chunks: And he asked him about a man who purchased cut fodder, then did not cut it and left it until it became barley, while he had stipulated with the landowner on the day he bought it that whatever misfortune came upon it would be upon the landowner. So he said:

If he stipulated with the landowner on the day he bought it that, if he wished, he could make it into ears, and if he wished, he could make it fodder, then his condition is binding for him. But if he did not stipulate that, then it is not proper for him to leave it until it becomes ears; and if he does so, then its tax and expense are upon him, and whatever comes out of it belongs to him.

key_terms.الْعِلْجِ: the non-Muslim landholder or cultivator referred to in the transaction
key_terms.سُنْبُلًا: grain in ear or spike form after further growth
key_terms.شَعِيرًا: barley after the crop has matured
key_terms.طَسْقَهُ: its land tax or due levy
key_terms.قَصِيلًا: fodder crop cut green for animal feed
key_terms.نَائِبَةٍ: an occurring mishap, loss, or adverse incident

ai.seo_question: If someone buys fodder crops and leaves them until they mature, who bears the tax and expenses in Shi'a fiqh?
ai.summary: This hadith gives a legal ruling about purchasing fodder crops and then leaving them to mature beyond the original intended use. If the buyer explicitly stipulated that he could either cut them as fodder or leave them to develop, his condition stands; otherwise, if he leaves them to mature, he becomes responsible for the associated tax and expenses while retaining the produce.

en.bab-ul-qaim-publications: Hadith.3869 - Sama'ah asked him about a man who purchased fodder crops but did not harvest them and left them until they turned into barley. He had stipulated with the landowner at the time of purchase that any incident or damage would be the responsibility of the landowner.

Imam (as) said: "If he stipulated with the landowner at the time of purchase that he may leave it to grow into spikes or cut it as fodder, then he is bound by his condition. However, if he did not stipulate this, it is not proper for him to leave it until it becomes spikes. If he does so, then he is responsible for its tax and expenses, and he is entitled to what it produces."
